transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start time: 14:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Ruiz (Redwood SE), Sofia Martinez (Head of ML, Lighthouse), Daniel Kim (Infra Lead), Priya Rao (Product PM)

Summary (auto): Discussed latency/throughput SLOs, benchmarking approach, and deployment options (hosted/dedicated/private). Identified next steps and owners.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Maya): okay hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, with Ethan our solutions engineer. how's everyone doing?
00:08 Speaker 2 (Sofia): good thanks, Sofia here, excited to dig in — we've been looking at latency for our recommendation streaming use case, so i pulled in daniel and priya.
00:14 Speaker 3 (Daniel): hey all, hi, infra questions mostly from me. we want to understand p95 targets and how they map to dedicated vs hosted.
00:22 Speaker 1 (Maya): perfect, that's the plan. quick agenda: p95 targets, concurrency, streaming behaviour (server-sent events / websockets), token/sec benchmarks and what we can run as a proof. ethan will cover the benchmark approach.
00:34 Speaker 4 (Ethan): cool thanks. quick question for you, sofia — what's your target p95 for short request path? like 1-2 turn product recs, ~50-150 tokens?
00:44 Speaker 2 (Sofia): for our realtime recs we want p95 around 100-150ms ideally. if we can't hit 100ms then at least under 200ms. for longer explainability responses we're okay with up to 400-500ms p95.
00:56 Speaker 3 (Daniel): and concurrency — we expect spikes to 500 concurrent streaming sessions during peak; baseline ~150. token rates vary but many sessions will stream at 10-20 tokens/sec.
01:08 Speaker 4 (Ethan): okay that helps. rough high-level: hosted API good for getting started; p95 depends on model choice, quantization and route. dedicated gives you pinned GPU pools and more predictable latency — we can guarantee tighter p95 in many cases because of reserved capacity and tail-latency controls.
01:28 Speaker 2 (Sofia): when you say p95 guarantee for dedicated, what's realistic for a small-ish model (~7B float or quantized 7B) for 50-150 token responses?
01:36 Speaker 4 (Ethan): from our internal benchmarks: on a gpus-rtx A100 / H100 class node, a quantized 7B with batching turned low and streaming enabled typically sees p95 around 80-120ms for short 100-token responses at moderate concurrency. but important caveats: sequence length, the model architecture, and KV cache hits change things. our numbers often have noise — those are ballpark.
01:58 Speaker 3 (Daniel): can you explain KV cache and prefix caching a bit? we have a lot of repeated prefixes for product context.
02:04 Speaker 4 (Ethan): sure — KV (key-value) cache keeps past token state in memory between requests so repeated prefixes can bypass recomputation. prefix caching helps a lot for chat-like repeated context. it can reduce token/sec cost and lower p95, but you need sticky routing or shared cache to benefit across instances.
02:28 Speaker 2 (Sofia): sticky routing concerns us a bit because we run in multi-az and want failover — does Redwood handle fallback if an instance with the cache goes down?
02:36 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes, we have automatic fallback policies to a compatible model variant or region; if sticky routing is required for cache we can do short TTLs and replicate KV across a few nodes to reduce downtime risk. we'll include design notes in the security pack.
02:52 Speaker 3 (Daniel): about streaming — do you support both SSE and websockets and what's the impact on p95 vs non-streamed responses?
02:59 Speaker 4 (Ethan): we support streaming over HTTP SSE and websocket-like flows in our SDK. streaming adds a little overhead per connection but reduces perceived latency because tokens arrive as soon as decoded. p95 for first token is usually lower than full completion p95. we typically measure p95 for first-token and for completion. important to align on which one you care about.
03:24 Speaker 2 (Priya): product question — we want the UI to show the first token within 60-80ms for a snappy experience. is that feasible?
03:32 Speaker 4 (Ethan): for first-token p95 60-80ms you likely need optimized model (7B quantized or a tuned 3B) + dedicated capacity with small batch windows + prefix caching. Hosted can do it sometimes but less predictable due to noisy neighbors.
03:46 Speaker 2 (Sofia): ok noted. can you run token/sec benchmarks for our profiles? we can provide a sample prompt set and concurrency distribution.
03:53 Speaker 4 (Ethan): yes we can. recommended approach: you send sample prompt set + concurrency mix; we'll run token/sec tests against hosted and dedicated-like setups, measure first-token p95, completion p95, tokens/sec, and tail latencies. we'll also include token cost estimates.
04:10 Speaker 3 (Daniel): about private / VPC option — we may need on-prem for some customers due to data residency. does private deployment change your latency profile?
04:18 Speaker 4 (Ethan): private can improve latency if you colocate near your infra and remove a public network hop, but you lose some of our managed autoscaling benefits unless you opt into our dedicated hardware. private also adds friction for kernel optimizations and rollout speed.
04:34 Speaker 2 (Sofia): security checklist — SOC2, SSO, RBAC, KMS?
04:39 Speaker 1 (Maya): yes we'll send the security pack: SOC2 summary, SAML/SSO options, RBAC, audit logs, KMS integration details (we support customer-managed KMS/HSM for private).
04:51 Speaker 2 (Priya): and what about monitoring? tracing hooks per route and per-token cost visibility?
04:55 Speaker 1 (Maya): Redwood Console exposes per-route latency histograms, token-level cost breakdowns, and tracing. we'll attach sample dashboards.
05:06 Speaker 4 (Ethan): a few more technical notes: quantization helps throughput and reduces memory; 4-bit quant often gives big gains but depends on model. also kernel selection and compilation matter for token/sec. our benchmark will include model variants and quant levels.
05:22 Speaker 3 (Daniel): are you able to do end-to-end benchmarks from our region (we run AWS us-east-1) to approximate real network latency?
05:28 Speaker 4 (Ethan): yes we can run tests from us-east-1. for hosted tests we'll measure with and without simulated network to isolate compute vs network. for dedicated we can run on a reserved pool in the same AZ.
05:42 Speaker 2 (Sofia): one concern: cost — if we pin dedicated nodes to hit p95, that could blow the cost. how do you suggest balancing cost vs latency?
05:50 Speaker 4 (Ethan): typical levers: batching policy (trade latency for throughput), cache effectiveness (reduce compute), model size & quantization, and routing (use cheaper model variants for non-critical routes). Redwood Optimize gives recommendations and expected unit cost delta.
06:06 Speaker 2 (Priya): do you have any public numbers we can look at for 7B and 13B models?
06:10 Speaker 1 (Maya): we'll include a benchmark sheet with 3-4 model points and p95/throughput numbers. note that numbers are indicative; we'll run a Lighthouse-specific run once we get your prompts.
06:22 Speaker 3 (Daniel): about concurrency — if we have 500 concurrent streaming sessions, what's the expected tokens/sec across the cluster? any rule of thumb?
06:29 Speaker 4 (Ethan): depends on tokens/sec per session; e.g., at 15 tokens/sec * 500 sessions = 7.5k tokens/sec. with batching and quantized 7B you might sustain that on a small fleet but you'd want autoscale headroom. we'll model this in the benchmark.
06:47 Speaker 2 (Sofia): and what about fallbacks in case of overload? we'd rather degrade to shorter answers than fail.
06:53 Speaker 1 (Maya): Redwood supports automatic degradation policies: shorter response length, switch to cheaper model variants, or queueing with backpressure. can set canary and A/B rollouts too.
07:06 Speaker 4 (Ethan): small note on measurement — we'll produce p50/p95/p99 and first-token vs completion. we also instrument tokens/sec and bytes/sec for streaming sessions.
07:18 Speaker 2 (Priya): ok this is great. timeline: we need numbers for an internal decision in 2 weeks.
07:22 Speaker 1 (Maya): we can aim to deliver the benchmark and pricing within one week if you send the prompt set and concurrency distribution today or tomorrow.
07:30 Speaker 2 (Sofia): i'll share the prompt set and a traffic shape. also sending anonymized traces.
07:34 Speaker 3 (Daniel): i'll follow up to scope VPC network requirements and what logs we need.
07:39 Speaker 1 (Maya): excellent. recap and next steps: ethan will run token/sec benchmarks and provide a runbook; maya will send pricing and security docs; sofia/daniel to provide prompts and SLO targets.
07:51 Speaker 2 (Priya): quick question — competitors; we've done a proof vs openai gpt-4o and sage maker baseline, any quick notes?
07:58 Speaker 4 (Ethan): qualitatively, OpenAI varies on tail latency and is less configurable about dedicated routing. SageMaker gives control but you manage kernels and optimization. Redwood sits between: managed runtime with ops optimizations and dedicated/private options.
08:14 Speaker 1 (Maya): any final Qs?
08:18 Speaker 2 (Sofia): none, thanks.
08:20 Speaker 3 (Daniel): nope thanks.
08:22 Speaker 1 (Maya): thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
